newsitem.title: USA: US bonds may rally before bears prevail, techs say.
newsitem.headline: US bonds may rally before bears prevail, techs say.

text.p: U.S. government securities charts show the market may face a corrective rally over the next few days which could push long-term Treasury yields back down to 7.0 percent, technical analysts said.
But the long-term trend remains bleak, chart pundits warned; many used the same catch-phrase -- "rally in a bear market" -- to dismiss any possible near-term rise in prices.
Walter Burke, technical analyst at consulting firm MCM MoneyWatch Inc, said he would view any rise in prices now as a retracement from a steep back up in yields since early August.
"We expect the retracement to kind of hold between 7.0 percent and 6.95 percent on the bond yield," Burke said.

"But then I would think the market would probably turn down again and actually take out the lows at 7.25 percent and go to 7-3/8 or maybe 7-1/2 (percent) eventually. It looks like the market is poised to do that," Burke said.
In the beginning of August, the yield on the Treasury's 30-year bond was hovering around 6.75 percent. In early afternoon on Wednesday, the bellwether was down 3/32 at 95-14/32 to yield 7.12 percent.
Analysts said the market is still in the process of correcting an oversold condition, which it has been holding for about three weeks now.
Chart analysts said Treasury prices could benefit from that movement in the very near term if players continue to square off previously-set short positions.
"The market has been oversold for quite some time now ... There is some room for an upward short-term correction here," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.

But some analysts said the market is still very tense going into some key economic indicators later this week, such as the August producer and consumer price indices and the August retail sales report.
They said a large liquidation of positions over the last two days, which prompted many investors to jump to the sidelines, is a clear indication of the market's anxiety.
"People attributed that to the delivery of futures," said Ron Peterson, a member of the government trading desk at Deustche Morgan Greenfell.

"However, the fact that people have chosen not to roll those positons tells me the market is at a very nervous state here," he said, adding he was "a little concerned" about the area above 7.18 percent on the bechmark bond yield.
The yield curve, which had flattened sharply last week, steepened a bit over the last days.
The spread between the two-year notes and the 30-year bond was around 78 basis points on Wednesday, against 74 points seen on September 4 and 85 points registered on August 20.
